Data were collected mainly from IDP camps in the districts Amuru and Gulu.

The qualitative psychological autopsy method we used is capable of generating rich and complex data about the lives of suicidal individuals by interviewing relatives and significant others about the deceased's lives and events leading to their death (Owens, Lambert, Lloyd, & Donavan, 2008). The basis for the narrative part was one broad question: Please describe the circumstances that surrounded the suicidal death of your (wife or husband or nephew and so on)?
Twenty decedents (17 men and 3 women) were identified, all aged between 18–39 years or 60–85 years.

evidence.section_title: Alcohol Influencing the Suicidal Process of Significant Others
evidence.quote: These increasing aggressive tendencies toward their spouses seemed to have contributed to the suicides of some of the women in our study as expressed in the following voices: "Alcohol made him aggressive; whenever he drank he became violent toward his wife . . ." (case16:informant3). And "they were living peacefully until our father had a very sudden change in his character. He could drink too much, come back [home] late and fight her, such behavior took about three months . . . and she died." They would fight every evening (case18:informant3). To other men, alcohol seemed to have facilitated revenge toward the deceased. For example, in one of our elderly decedents, suicide followed mistreatment by his son (see Kizza, Knizek, Kinyanda, & Hjelmeland, in press).
The data were part of a qualitative psychological autopsy study aimed at understanding suicide in post conflict Northern Uganda.

Background: Alcohol has been noted to be an important factor in nearly 68% of the suicides in Northern Uganda, yet exactly how alcohol contributes to suicide in this region. Methods: Qualitative psychological autopsy interviews were conducted with bereaved relatives and friends of 20 suicides mainly from Internally Displaced Peoples' camps in Northern Uganda. Data were analyzed using a modified Interpretative Phenomenological analysis (IPA). Results: Alcohol had a direct or an indirect influence on the suicide of 16 out of the 20 decedents. Directly, alcohol facilitated the suicidal process, was a means to suicide, or had an influence on the decedents' lifestyles. Indirectly, alcohol had an influence on the suicidal process of the deceased through the drinking behavior of significant others. Conclusions: This study established that alcohol not only contributes to the suicidal process of the individuals through acute and chronic alcohol consumption, but also through victimization of those lowest in the power hierarchy by alcohol abusers higher up in the power hierarchy. Therefore, future development of suicide prevention programs should address the interrelated public health problem of alcohol abuse.

Alcohol had a direct or an indirect influence on the suicidal death of the decedents. Directly, it had an influence on the suicidal process by facilitating the suicidal acts; it was used as a means to suicide or had an influence on the overall life style of the individuals. Indirectly, alcohol had an influence in the suicidal process of the decedents as victims of the alcohol use by others.

In this study we explored the role of alcohol in suicide in postconflict Northern Uganda. The findings indicated that alcohol acted as a facilitator of suicidal acts, was used as a means to implement the act, or had an influence on the overall lifestyle of some of the decedents who abused alcohol. It further influenced the suicidal process of significant others as victims of those who misuse alcohol.

Our results show that alcohol played a complex role in the suicide cases studied. In two of our groups, alcohol could be seen as a method of suicide, while in the other groups it had a more indirect influence by causing intra- and interpersonal suffering.
